Senses.Explanation: The records define straight mind against bends, twists, crookedness, and falseness: ‘straight mind means without bends or twists.’ Literally, a straight or straightforward mind. The term occurs 163 times in 89 allowed texts. The corpus supplies two compact definitions: 'straight mind means without bends or twists' (直心者，無委曲故), and 'straight mind is the site of the Way because it has no falseness' (直心是道場，無虛假故). The Platform Record repeats 'straight mind is the site; straight mind is the clean land' (直心是道場，直心是淨土), then contrasts inwardly acting crookedly while verbally speaking straight with actually carrying out straight mind. Its positive clause is 'only carry out straight mind; regarding all things, have no grasping' (但行直心，於一切法上，無有執著). Another address expands the pattern into four coordinated expressions: 'straight mind is the site; straight speech is the subtle teaching; straight conduct is subtle conduct; straight verification is the subtle result' (直心是道場，直說是妙法，直行是妙行，直證是妙果). The common collocation 'straight mind and straight conduct' (直心直行) occurs 24 times in 17 texts. One record describes it by the absence of self-versus-other, right-versus-wrong, falseness, and crookedness; another uses 'straight mind, straight conduct, original color, original share' (直心直行，本色本分) to characterize a named Chan figure's meetings with people.

Senses.Explanation: Pei Xiu (裴休) is the Tang official whom Chan records deploy as a lay questioner, patron, student of Huangbo Xiyun, and preface writer. He visits Hualin Shanjue and questions him after two tigers answer Hualin Shanjue's call. Other records show Huangbo loudly calling 'Pei Xiu!' and questioning where he is, and later using the same name as the answer when Pei asks him to name a painted Buddha. Three lamp compilations also transmit Pei's preface on the damage caused when inherited teachings become competing doorways and weapons. Those parallel prefaces are one event, while the two added Huangbo exchanges supply distinct public uses of his name.

Senses.Explanation: The imperative reverses illumination from outward pursuit toward shining back. Stored cases command return, looking beneath one’s own feet, or attach a complement such as “illuminating past and present.” This written form occurs 50 times in 35 allowed texts; the common variant 'turn the light around and shine back' (回光返照) occurs 168 times in 97 texts, and the reversed order 'shine back and turn the light' (返照回光) occurs 16 times. The Record of the Transmission of the Lamp gives the literal instruction, 'turn the light around and shine back; look: what are body and mind?' (迴光返照看身心是何物). Shitou's Grass Hut Song says, 'turn the light around and shine back, then return' (迴光返照便歸來). Linji tells his listeners that at the words they should 'themselves turn the light around and shine back, seeking nothing else' (便自迴光返照，更不別求). Chengtian Cique says, 'only turn the light around and shine back; carefully search beneath your own heels and look what it is' (但自迴光返照，向自己脚根下子細推尋，看是箇什麼). Gongchen Jueke closes an address with 'each of you, please turn the light around and shine back; do not hesitate further' (各請迴光返照，休更踟躕). Fenyang's verse supplies a result-clause: 'turn the light around and shine back, illuminating present and past' (迴光返照明今古). The corpus thus records an imperative verb phrase, a poetic return, a prohibition on seeking elsewhere, and direct objects or complements such as body and mind, beneath one's heels, and present and past. Zhongfeng Mingben explicitly singles out “the four characters (回光返照),” then says merely sitting quietly with closed eyes is not what he names. This is his attested description and falsification, not a universal prescription. Miyun’s reversed (返照回光) remains a related phrase only.
